diagnostic_evidence.quote: \Pi(x, t) = \frac{1}{t} \Lambda(x) + \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \wedge E(x),
(h_z)_* \pi = \frac{1}{z} \pi \quad \text{for all } z \in \mathbb{R}^\times.
the symplectic form $\omega=\Pi^{-1}$ satisfies $h_z^* \omega = z\omega$

issues.failure_explanation: With h_z(x,t)=(x,zt) and the standard pushforward used elsewhere in the paper (Prop. prop:added-3, Appendix B), dh_z(\partial_t)=z\partial_t and the coefficient 1/t at the image point becomes z/t'. Hence (h_z)_*\Pi = z\Pi, not z^{-1}\Pi. The two definitions are also mutually incompatible. If \omega=\pi^{-1} satisfies h_z^*\omega=z\omega, then (h_z)_*\omega=z^{-1}\omega and so (h_z)_*\pi=z\pi. The remark's claim about the symplectization therefore contradicts the Poisson-homogeneity definition.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Fix the convention, e.g. define homogeneous Poisson by (h_z)_*\pi = z\pi (equivalently L_Z\pi=-\pi), consistent with h_z^*\omega=z\omega. Then redo the one-line computation.
issues.overall_effect: The stated defining condition for homogeneous Poisson manifolds is not met by the Poissonization, and the Poisson and symplectic notions of homogeneity disagree.
issues.title: Poissonization does not satisfy the stated homogeneity law; homogeneity conventions are inconsistent
issues.why_classification: Correcting the convention and the computation is local, and every later use (the symplectization, homogeneity of sprays) survives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the symplectic form $\Omega = \int_0^1(\phi^s_X)^*\omega_{can} ds$ is also $1$-homogeneous
Suppose $\omega_0,\ \omega_1$ are two $1$-homogeneous symplectic forms on $M$, for which $(\omega_0)_{|N} =(\omega_1)_{|N}
such that $i^*\omega_0 = i^*\omega_1 = 0$ ($X$ is Lagrangian for both)
From the homogeneity of $\Psi$ and $\phi^s_X$ we get

issues.failure_explanation: The spray X vanishes on the zero section, but its linearization there maps a vertical vector \delta\xi to (s\pi^\sharp\delta\xi, \delta\xi). Hence at points of the zero section (\phi^s_X)^*\omega_{can}(\delta\xi_1,\delta\xi_2)=\pm 2s\pi(\delta\xi_1,\delta\xi_2), and integrating gives \Omega=\pm\pi on vertical vectors, while \omega_{can} vanishes on them. So (\omega_{can})|_N \neq \Omega|_N wherever \pi\neq0, and the hypothesis of thm: Darboux-Weinstein fails. The map \Psi on which the proof of thm: bi-realization rests is therefore not justified.

failure_location.quote: By the homogeneous Darboux-Weinstein Theorem (\ref{thm: Darboux-Weinstein}), there exists $\Psi:T^*P\rightarrow T^*P$ such that $\omega_{can} = \Psi^*\Omega$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Note that the zero section is Lagrangian for both \Omega and \omega_{can}, since \phi^s_X fixes it pointwise. Then apply the paper's homogeneous Weinstein Lagrangian neighborhood theorem (thm: Weinstein lagrangian) instead, which yields an equivariant \Psi fixing the zero section.
issues.overall_effect: The existence of the homogeneous Karasev-type bi-realization (canonical form, deformed source and target) is unsupported as argued.
issues.title: Darboux-Weinstein theorem applied although Omega and omega_can differ along the zero section
issues.why_classification: The correct tool is already in the paper and its hypotheses are routinely checked, and the conclusion is unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we call variation functions to any time-dependent functions $(f_s)_{s\in I}$ such that $df_s = \xi_s$, for all $s\in I$.
There exists $(\mathcal{H}_s)_s$ a time-dependent homogeneous Hamiltonian such that

issues.failure_explanation: Variation functions are defined as any primitives, so they are determined only up to locally constant c(s). If f_s is a 1-homogeneous primitive, then f_s+c is also a variation function, but h_z^*(f_s+c)=zf_s+c\neq z(f_s+c) for c\neq0. The direction 'xi_s 1-homogeneous implies f_s 1-homogeneous' is therefore false. No proof is given.

failure_location.quote: Then $\xi_s$ are $1$-homogeneous if and only if $f_s$ are $1$-homogeneous.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State instead that 1-homogeneous exact \xi_s admit a unique 1-homogeneous primitive, e.g. f_s=\iota_Z\xi_s since \xi_s=L_Z\xi_s=d\iota_Z\xi_s. Use this normalized choice of variation functions.
issues.overall_effect: The step that variation functions of homogeneous families serve as homogeneous Hamiltonians (needed for the hPHI) is not justified as stated.
issues.title: Homogeneity of variation forms does not imply homogeneity of arbitrary variation functions
issues.why_classification: A one-line normalization of the primitive restores everything that is used later.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the induced diffeomorphism $\phi_L:P_J\rightarrow P_J$ is a homogeneous Poisson diffeomorphism;
And so, any bisection induces a homogeneous diffeomorphism of the unit manifold $M$

issues.failure_explanation: Equivariance of \alpha|_L^{-1} requires L to be T^*h-invariant, which is not assumed. For example, a non-invariant Lagrangian bisection near the unit, such as the graph of \epsilon dF with F not 1-homogeneous, induces a Poisson diffeomorphism approximating the flow of X_F. That flow is not equivariant, so item (1) fails as stated.

failure_location.quote: If a bisection $L\subset \Sigma$ is Lagrangian, then:

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis that L is a homogeneous (T^*h-invariant) Lagrangian bisection. The later constructions use only such bisections.
issues.overall_effect: The homogeneity conclusion of item (1), and the preceding remark, hold only for homogeneous bisections.
issues.title: Missing homogeneity hypothesis on the Lagrangian bisection
issues.why_classification: Adding a standard local hypothesis preserves all intended uses.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the induced map $\varphi_L = \beta\circ \alpha^{-1}_{|L}$ defines a Poisson diffeomorphism
\phi^s_H = \alpha\circ \phi^s_{\alpha^*H}\circ \sigma,
the fibers of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are symplectic orthogonal to each other.

issues.failure_explanation: By symplectic orthogonality, X_{\alpha^*H} is tangent to the \beta-fibers, so its flow preserves \beta. For g=\phi^s_{\alpha^*H}(\sigma(x)) this gives \beta(g)=x, and by item 2 \alpha(g)=\phi^s_H(x). Hence \beta\circ(\alpha|_{L_s})^{-1}=(\phi^s_H)^{-1}=\phi^{-s}_H, contradicting item 3.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either use \varphi_L=\alpha\circ(\beta|_L)^{-1} or state \varphi_{L_s}=\phi^{-s}_H (equivalently use L_{-s}). Adjust the integrator remark accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: With the paper's conventions, the integrator x -> \beta\circ(\alpha|_{L_{\Delta t}})^{-1}(x) approximates the backward flow.
issues.title: Item 3 identifies the bisection map with the forward flow, but the definitions give the inverse flow
issues.why_classification: A consistent time-orientation or convention fix restores the statement without new arguments.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $\phi_\epsilon$ is a Jacobi diffeomorphism\footnote
\phi\circ \{f,g\}_{J_1} = \{\phi\circ f,\phi\circ g\}_{J_2}.
Then we can transport the original Hamilton function $H(x)$ to the homogeneous Poisson manifold considering $H^P(x,t) = tH(x)$.
suitable for incorporating time-dependent, dissipative and thermodynamic phenomena.

issues.failure_explanation: From \Pi=\Lambda/t+\partial_t\wedge E, the vector field X^P_{tH} has \partial_t-component \mp tE(H)\partial_t. Its equivariant flow is therefore (x,t)->(\phi(x),a(x)t) with a\neq1 when E(H)\neq0. Such a map descends to a conformal Jacobi map, not to a bracket-preserving Jacobi diffeomorphism as the footnote requires. Conversely, Hamiltonian flows preserve (\Lambda,E) only if E(\mathcal{H}_s)\Lambda=0, which at s=0 forces E(H^J)=0 (e.g. Reeb-invariant contact Hamiltonians). So JHIs as defined do not exist for genuinely dissipative Hamiltonians. The paper also gives no argument beyond citing the category equivalence, whose morphisms are line-bundle (conformal) maps.

failure_location.quote: we can conclude that we have a $1$-to-$1$ correspondence between homogeneous Poisson Hamiltonian integrators and Jacobi Hamiltonian integrators. This grants the existence of JHI's, constructed as explained above.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redefine JHIs using conformal Jacobi diffeomorphisms (Jacobi automorphisms of the trivial line bundle). Then prove that homogeneous Poisson diffeomorphisms and homogeneous Hamiltonian flows of tH descend to conformal Jacobi maps and Jacobi Hamiltonian flows, with matching order.
issues.overall_effect: The main conclusion (existence of JHIs and their one-to-one correspondence with hPHIs) is false or unsupported in the advertised dissipative regime. The prose claims that Jacobi structure is preserved are also unreliable.
issues.title: JHIs defined via strict Jacobi diffeomorphisms; the claimed correspondence with hPHIs and existence fail for dissipative Hamiltonians
issues.why_classification: The guarantee type of the central definition must change, and the correspondence needs a new descent argument; as stated, the advertised dissipative scope is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $\mathcal{H}_s = H^J + o(s^{k-1})$,
since to preserving the Poisson structure and the Hamiltonian (up to a certain order)
X_H = \Lambda(\cdot,dH) - HE(\cdot)

issues.failure_explanation: The definitions only require the integrator to be the flow of a Hamiltonian agreeing with H to order k, so H is approximated, not preserved. Moreover, even the exact Jacobi flow does not conserve H, since X_H(H) = \Lambda(dH,dH) - HE(H) = -HE(H), which is nonzero in dissipative cases.

failure_location.quote: This approach preserves not only the Jacobi structure and the Hamiltonian, but also the induced foliation and Casimir functions

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the claim with 'approximates the Hamiltonian dynamics to order k', noting that H itself is not conserved by Jacobi flows.
issues.overall_effect: It misstates the guarantee delivered by the method.
issues.title: Conclusion claims the method preserves the Hamiltonian
issues.why_classification: Rewording to the supported claim affects no formal result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We want to prove that $\pi_*(h_z^*(\alpha)) = h_z^*(\pi_*(\alpha)).$
We recall that the action of $\mathbb{R}^\times$ on $P$ is free and proper
If $N$ is a point, then we can find a contractible neighborhood of $N$, and $\beta$ is given by the homogeneous Poincar\'e Lemma.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof only shows that fiber integration commutes with h_z^* for the action extended trivially in the homotopy parameter. It never constructs the contracting homotopy, whose radial contraction cannot commute with a free \mathbb{R}^\times-action, and never shows exactness or homogeneity of the primitive. Also, for the free action t->zt (t\neq0) no invariant open set is star-shaped, since the segment from (x,t) to (x,-t) meets t=0. The lemma's only use (N a point) is likewise vacuous.

failure_location.quote: Let $U$ be a homogeneous star-shaped open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, then all $1$-homogeneous closed $p$-forms are exact and their primitive is also homogeneous.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the argument with the global identity \omega = L_Z\omega = d(\iota_Z\omega) for 1-homogeneous closed \omega (Z=t\partial_t), which gives a 1-homogeneous primitive with no star-shaped hypothesis.
issues.overall_effect: The stated lemma is unsupported as proved.
issues.title: Homogeneous Poincare lemma: vacuous hypothesis and a proof that never establishes exactness
issues.why_classification: A one-line standard argument proves a stronger version, and nothing downstream is lost.
